newsitem.title: FRANCE: French parliament wrestles over immigration bill.
newsitem.headline: French parliament wrestles over immigration bill.

text.p: French Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre defended a disputed bill to combat illegal immigration as a rampart against racism and xenophobia on Tuesday as parliament began a final reading amid fresh protests.
In an acrimonious debate punctuated by incessant heckling, Socialist opposition floor leader Laurent Fabius attacked the proposed law as "ineffectual, dangerous and Kafkaesque".

He accused the conservative government of seeking to implement part of the extreme-right National Front's platform in the hope of "appeasing the evil beast", while at the same time shelving a bill to strengthen the fight against racism.
"Beware! The apple rarely eats the worm," he said.
Fabius said the bill would turn all foreigners, and their French hosts, into suspects and pledged that a left-wing government would repeal the law as one of its first priorities.
Debre insisted that the bill to tighten controls and make it easier to expel illegal aliens was "balanced" and accused left-wing critics of "lies, hypocrisy and manipulation".
"If we want to integrate foreigners into the national community, if we want to turn back racism and xenophobia in this country, we have to fight illegal immigration," he declared.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe said in an article in the newspaper Le Monde that the bill's critics were playing into the hands of the National Front by blurring the distinction between legal and illegal immigration.
In a radio interview earlier, Debre used an argument often brandished by Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, suggesting that recent immigrants were welfare scroungers.

He said the nature of immigration into France had changed in the last few years from "workers who wanted to integrate into the national community to claimants who want to take advantage of our welfare system and don't want to integrate".

Parliament's legal committee has removed the bill's most fiercely contested clause, which would have required hosts to report to the police when foreign guests subject to visa requirements left their homes.

Instead, foreigners on short-term visas will be required to report their own departure to the authorities, and government prefects instead of local mayors will be responsible for issuing "accommodation certificates".

But intellectuals and artists campaigning against the bill, who led an estimated 100,000-strong demonstration in Paris on Saturday, held a fresh protest outside parliament to demand the complete withdrawal of the legislation.
Organisers said 30,000 people braved wind and rain to march to parliament. Police said 16,000 people took part. A few thousand demonstrated in Marseille, Toulouse, Rennes, and Nice.
"This parliament is in the process of destroying French citizenship," actor Michel Piccoli, himself a son of Italian immigrants, told reporters in Paris.

The opposition Socialists and Communists, largely absent when the Assembly first debated the bill in December, submitted a welter of motions to delay or amend the bill and the National Assembly debate was expected to last three days.
Their tactics had no chance of success since the ruling coalition holds four-fifths of the 577 assembly seats.

Among the measures are an extension of the period for which illegal aliens may be held without trial, the right for police to search vehicles up to 20 km (12 miles) from borders and a provision allowing police to raid illegal workshops.

The National Front's number two, Bruno Megret, dismissed the amended bill in a statement as a "political fraud", which he said showed the government was impotent in combating immigration and weak-kneed towards what he called the "human rights lobby".
Debre noted opinion polls showed a clear majority of up to 69 percent of voters support his bill.
He said critics had created the impression that it would affect the 80 million foreigners who visit France each year whereas if would only affect some 150,000 people.

The French government meanwhile told the European Parliament to mind its own business and not interfere in France's internal affairs after it narrowly adopted a resolution last week which urged the bill's withdrawal.
